answer: Yes. The story uses sophisticated metaphors to illuminate class, power, and belonging. Miss Emily’s attention is “inventory,” revealing how her business instincts shape her relationships. Marnie feels she has been “shown a door and told, in the same breath, which side of it she lived on,” capturing recognition that simultaneously reinforces exclusion. The comparison of mutual usefulness to hands supporting opposite ends of a heavy table gives the story’s ambivalent view of intimacy a concrete, resonant form. Regional expressions such as “ain’t” also function as markers of identity and class pressure, rather than merely adding local color.
